newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Five MPs quit in row with Portugal rightist leader.
newsitem.headline: Five MPs quit in row with Portugal rightist leader.

text.p: Manuel Monteiro, embattled leader of Portugal's third biggest party, appeared back in control of his right-wing Popular Party (PP) on Wednesday after five rebel MPs resigned from parliament.

The lanky 34-year-old lawyer led the "Eurosceptical" PP to triple its vote in October 1995 general elections but a personality clash with firebrand, former newspaper editor Paulo Portas later threatened to tear the party apart.
Portas, who criticised Monteiro's autocratic style, announced his resignation as an MP on Tuesday night and his allies, who held a third of the PP's 15 seats, followed suit.
Last month Monteiro quit as the PP's leader after four years in charge and said he would not stand again at an extraordinary party congress in December.
However, analysts said the door was open for Monteiro to seek re-election now that his rivals were out of the way.
"There's nobody else in the party to come forward," said a Western diplomat. "Monteiro has got rid of the bulk of the movers and shakers in the party."

The PP is the joint third largest party in the 230-seat parliament. The ruling Socialists, who are four seats short of an absolute majority, have 112 seats and the centre-right Social Democratic Party (PSD) have 88. The Communists (PCP) have 15.
Portas told the SIC television station on Tuesday night that he would not stand against Monteiro for the party leadership.
"I don't have the right conditions, in terms of loyalty or my political work, to continue in the parliamentary group," he told Publico paper in an interview published on Wednesday.

Portas suspended his parliamentary mandate last month after withdrawing his sole candidacy in an election for the leadership of the party's parliamentary group. Eight of his colleagues abstained and only seven voted for him.

The resignation of Portas and former television newsreader Manuela Moura Guedes, former newspaper owner Luis Nobre Guedes, lawyer Antonio Lobo Xavier and businessman Manuel Silva Carvalho, would not affect the balance of power in Portugal.
Their places in parliament would eventually be taken over by other members of the PP who were runners-up in party lists in the last elections under the proportional representation system.
Monteiro, a clear articulator of his party's policies, boosted the PP's share of the vote to nine percent in October 1995 from four percent at the 1991 election.
The PP wants to hold a referendum on revision of the Maastricht treaty, criticises the border-free Schengen agreement and says it would tighten restrictions on agricultural imports.
